To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

under very broad conditions, the pathwise average cost per unit time for the random sampling approximating algorithms goes to the limit obtained if the ideal values were used, as time and the approximation parameters go to their respective limits.
, as time goes on, the average pathwise error for the approximating algorithm converges to the average pathwise cost that would be incurred by the optimal filter if it were used.

the pathwise errors per unit time of a wide class of random sampling approximations converge to the same limiting value as one would obtain if the optimal filter were used and the approximating processes and observations were replaced by their actual values.
In summary, our research is concerned with

approximating nonlinear filters that are of interest in a very long time horizon, and with the convergence of the average errors per unit time to a limit, which is just what one gets if the approximating filters are replaced by the optimal filters and the optimal filters are applied to the ideal signal and observation processes.
the construction of filters that can be used in practice over a long time period, where the optimal filter can be constructed.
approximating the optimal filter over an infinite time interval and, in particular, with showing that the approximating filter converges in the pathwise average cost to that of an optimal filter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, as the approximation parameter and time go to their limits in any way at al, the average pathwise error per time unit of a random sampling algorithm, which is a function of the approximation parameter, the time and the signal, noise and observation processes, converges to the average pathwise errors of the optimal filter.
, for a large class of approximating algorithms, as time, bandwidth and approximation parameter go to their limits in any way at al

the pathwise error converges to the same limit as the ideal filter would produce as time goes to its limit and the approximation parameter converges to its limit in whatever way is appropriate, and that the limit is independent of the way in which the time and approximation parameters converge to their limits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, under quite broad conditions on the signal and observation models, the pathwise average approximation errors for a large class of nonlinear filters, over a long time, converge to their limit as the time interval and approximation parameter go to their limit, regardless of the rate at which they go to infinity.

the pathwise error converges to the optimal error as time, approximation parameters, etc. converge to their limit in an arbitrary way, provided that the filter approximation and sampling parameters converge to their limit at a rate that is at least linear in time.

the pathwise error for a very wide class of approximating filters, including random sampling approximations, converges to the pathwise error that one would get if one used the optimal filter and ideal approximating processes, as time goes off to infinity and the approximations are made more precise in any way whatsoever.
The main takeaway from our work is that
one does not need to worry about the details of a specific approximation algorithm when one is concerned about the long term performance of a filter.
one can use a wide class of approximations that are computationally feasible, and still obtain the same asymptotic behavior that is obtained with the optimal filter.
the pathwise errors of the random sampling algorithms are asymptotically equivalent to the errors of the optimal filter.
